title: Being aware: how you notice the world, and what it is like to be you

summary.text: The fan hums all evening, yet most of the time you do not hear it. Being aware means knowing or feeling that something is there. Your attention picks out a few of the many sounds, sights and touches around you. In this unit you test how many sounds you notice when you are busy and when you sit still. You also taste the same lemon as your family and find out whether everyone feels the same sour. Then you meet the other beings who notice their world, and the big question nobody has answered: how does being aware happen at all?
summary.art: A girl of 7 sitting still on a mat in a flat with her eyes shut, one hand raised with fingers counting, while a ceiling fan turns, a crow sits on the window ledge and a gecko rests on the wall.

intro.hook: Can you hear the fan right now? Could you hear it a minute ago?
intro.text: Stop and listen for ten seconds. You may hear the fan, the fridge, a horn on the road or a bird. Most of these sounds were there before you stopped. You were not noticing them. Being aware of something means you know or feel that it is there. So what decides which sounds you are aware of?
intro.art: A child pausing over a notebook, eyes looking up, with small sound marks coming from a ceiling fan, a fridge and an open window.

outcomes: By the end I can say what being aware of something means.
By the end I can show, with my own test, that I notice more sounds when I pay attention.
By the end I can explain why I stop noticing a steady sound, and why I notice when it stops.
By the end I can say why nobody else can have my experience, and how we share experiences in words.
By the end I can tell being awake, dreaming and deep sleep apart.
By the end I can name other beings who notice their world, and say what scientists still argue about.

terms.meaning: Being aware of something means you know or feel that it is there.
terms.example: When you feel a mosquito on your arm, you are aware of the mosquito.
terms.art: A girl looking down at a mosquito on her arm, eyebrows raised.

terms.meaning: Consciousness is being aware of anything at all: sights, sounds, feelings or thoughts.
terms.example: When you wake up in the morning, your consciousness of the room comes back.
terms.art: A child waking up in bed and looking at a window full of morning light.

terms.meaning: To notice something is to become aware of it.
terms.example: You notice the pressure cooker when it whistles.
terms.art: A boy turning his head towards a whistling pressure cooker on a stove.

terms.meaning: Attention is choosing what to notice, out of everything around you.
terms.example: When you read a story, your attention is on the story, so you may not hear your name.
terms.art: A girl reading a book on a sofa while her mother calls from the doorway.

terms.meaning: An experience is what something is like for you: how it looks, sounds, tastes or feels to you.
terms.example: The sour of a lemon on your tongue is your experience. Nobody else can have it for you.
terms.art: A girl tasting lemon juice from a steel spoon, with her face screwed up.

terms.meaning: Your senses are how your body takes in the world: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching, and more.
terms.example: Your ears take in the sound of rain on the window.
terms.art: A child's face with small pictures beside the eyes, ears, nose, tongue and fingertips.

terms.meaning: Getting used to something means you stop noticing it because it goes on and on. Scientists call this habituation.
terms.example: After a few minutes in a room, you stop noticing the smell of the incense.
terms.art: A family sitting in a room with a thin line of incense smoke, everyone busy and not looking at it.

terms.meaning: A dream is what you are aware of during sleep: pictures, sounds and stories your sleeping mind makes.
terms.example: You might dream you are riding an elephant through Mysuru.
terms.art: A child asleep with a cloud above their head showing them riding an elephant past a palace.

explanations.context: This card says what being aware means.
explanations.definition: Being aware of something means knowing or feeling that it is there. Scientists call being aware of anything at all consciousness.
explanations.description: Right now you are aware of these words. You may also be aware of your feet on the floor, now that you read this. A moment ago you probably were not. Being aware is the most familiar thing there is, because it is there in every moment you are awake. Yet nobody can see your awareness from the outside. Other people can only see what you do and hear what you say.
examples: You are aware of a horn when you hear it on the road.
You are aware of feeling hungry before lunch.
You are aware of a thought, such as 'I want to play'.
explanations.art: A girl sitting on a floor mat, with small pictures around her of the things she is aware of: a book, her toes, a sound from the window and a thought bubble with a ball.

explanations.context: This card explains the sound test, where you counted sounds while busy and while sitting still.
explanations.definition: Attention is choosing what to notice. Your senses take in far more than you notice, and attention picks out a small part.
explanations.description: In the sound test, the room made the same sounds in the busy minutes and the still minutes. When you were racing to sort beans, your attention was on the beans. So you noticed only a few sounds. When you sat still and listened, your attention was on sounds. So you noticed many more. Your ears were working the whole time. What changed was where your attention was.
examples: While you watch cartoons, you may not hear Amma call you.
In a busy market, you hear your own name even through all the noise.
When you look for a red pencil, red things seem to jump out at you.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: a girl sorting beans with only one sound mark reaching her, and the same girl sitting still with eyes shut and many sound marks around her.

explanations.context: This card explains why you stop hearing the fan, and why you notice when it stops.
explanations.definition: When a sound, a smell or a touch goes on without changing, you stop noticing it. This is called getting used to it, or habituation. A change makes you notice again.
explanations.description: The fan hums all evening, and after a while you stop hearing it. The sound still reaches your ears. Your mind lets a steady sound fade into the background, so you can notice new things. When the fan suddenly stops, the change is new, so you notice it at once. This is why a power cut makes a flat feel suddenly quiet.
examples: You stop smelling your own home, but visitors notice its smell.
You stop feeling your watch or bangle on your wrist.
You notice the fridge only when its hum stops.
explanations.art: A flat in a power cut, with a fan slowing down and a girl looking up in surprise at the sudden quiet.

explanations.concept: What it is like to be you
explanations.context: This card explains the lemon test, where everyone tasted the same lemon juice.
explanations.definition: Your experience is what something is like for you. Only you have your experience. Others learn about it from your words, your face and what you do.
explanations.description: In the lemon test, everyone tasted the same lemon juice. Yet people often showed different numbers of fingers for the sour. Even when two people both show four fingers, nobody can be sure their sours feel the same. You cannot step inside another person's tongue to check. So we share our experiences by telling each other about them.
examples: You and your friend both say a mango is sweet, but each of you has your own sweet.
A song can make one person happy and another person sad.
A cold floor may feel nice to you and too cold to an older person.
explanations.art: Three family members each tasting lemon juice from a steel spoon, each with a different face and a different number of fingers held up.

explanations.context: This card explains the three ways of being aware in a day and a night.
explanations.definition: When you are awake, you are aware of the world around you. When you dream, you are aware of a world your sleeping mind makes. In deep sleep you are aware of very little, and later you remember almost nothing of it.
explanations.description: Every night you go through deep sleep and dreaming sleep several times. In a dream, strange things can feel normal, such as flying or talking to a fish. While you dream, the dream usually feels real. Almost everyone dreams every night, even people who remember no dreams. Doctors can also make a person unaware for an operation, with medicines called anaesthetics. Afterwards the person remembers nothing of the operation.
examples: Awake: you hear Amma call and you answer.
Dreaming: you swim through the sky among the clouds.
Deep sleep: the night passes, and in the morning it feels as if no time went by.
explanations.art: Three panels: a child awake brushing their teeth, the same child asleep with a dream cloud, and the same child in deep sleep under a dark blue sky with no cloud.

explanations.context: This card is about the other beings who notice their world.
explanations.description: Every living being notices their world in their own way. An ant notices the smell of food. A crow notices you at the window. A tulsi plant notices which way the light comes from, and grows towards it. Some thinkers say awareness does not need a brain, and that it runs through everything, down to the smallest particle. Scientists still argue about which beings are aware, and how.
examples: A touch-me-not plant folds up when touched. In 2018, scientists found that the medicines that make people unaware for an operation also stop the touch-me-not from folding.
In tests at Queen Mary University of London, led by Samadi Galpayage, young bumblebees rolled small balls again and again, even though they got no food for it.
A dog notices the sound of your footsteps before you open the door.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who signed the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness, 2024
perspectives.explanation: There is strong evidence that mammals and birds are aware, and a real chance that fish, octopuses, crabs and insects are too.
Awareness is something brains do. Plants have no brain. Plants do sense and respond, but these scientists say that happens automatically, without awareness.

perspectives.who: Plant scientists such as Monica Gagliano, and thinkers such as Philip Goff
perspectives.explanation: Sensing, choosing and remembering happen in plants too. Some thinkers say every bit of the world has some awareness.

explanations.art: A kitchen floor with an ant near a crumb, a crow on the window ledge, a tulsi plant leaning to the light and a child watching them all.

agreed.text: You notice only a small part of what your senses take in. Attention picks out what you notice.
agreed.evidence: In 1999, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked people to count ball passes in a short film. About half of them did not notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the middle.

agreed.text: You stop noticing a sound, smell or touch that goes on without changing, and you notice when it changes.
agreed.evidence: Many people say that they stop smelling their own home and notice the quiet when a fan or fridge stops. Experiments on habituation show the same in many animals, including us.

agreed.text: Almost everyone dreams every night, even people who say they never dream.
agreed.evidence: In sleep laboratories since the 1950s, people woken during dreaming sleep usually say they were having a dream, including people who remember no dreams at home.

agreed.text: Doctors can make a person unaware for an operation and then bring their awareness back.
agreed.evidence: Anaesthetics have been used for operations since the 1840s. People wake up afterwards and remember nothing of the operation.

challenging.context: This card is about what we notice.
challenging.claim: We see and hear everything that is in front of us.
challenging.for: The world looks full and complete to us, so it feels as if we take in all of it.
challenging.against: In the gorilla film test, about half the people did not see a gorilla walking past. In the sound test, you named far fewer sounds when you were busy.

challenging.context: This card is about sounds we are not paying attention to.
challenging.claim: Sounds you are not paying attention to are shut out completely, like a closed door.
challenging.who: Donald Broadbent, a British scientist, in 1958
challenging.for: In Colin Cherry's tests in 1953, people could say almost nothing about a message in the ear they were not listening to.
challenging.against: Neville Moray found in 1959 that some people heard their own name in the ear they were not listening to. Anne Treisman showed in 1960 that some meaning from that ear gets through.

challenging.context: This card is about who is aware.
challenging.who: Many people in the past, and some today
challenging.for: Only humans can tell us in words what they experience.
challenging.against: Other animals play, feel pain and learn. In 2024, many scientists signed the New York Declaration, saying there is strong evidence that mammals and birds are aware.

challenging.context: This card is about whether awareness needs a brain.
challenging.for: Medicines and injuries that change the brain change a person's awareness.
challenging.against: Plants sense, remember and choose. The medicines that make people unaware also stop a touch-me-not folding, though she has no brain.

big_questions.q: When you and a grown-up at home hear the same pressure cooker whistle, do you hear the same sound?
big_questions.hint: The same sound reaches both of you. But each of you has your own experience of it. How could you ever check?

big_questions.q: When you stop noticing the fan, where does its sound go?
big_questions.hint: When a fan stops, you notice at once. How could you know it had stopped, if you were not hearing it?

big_questions.q: What is it like to be an ant on the kitchen floor?
big_questions.hint: An ant smells and feels the floor through their feelers and feet. Their world is full of smells you cannot sense.

big_questions.q: In a dream, who is noticing the dream?
big_questions.hint: Your body is lying still in bed. Yet something is aware of the dream.

big_questions.q: In deep sleep you remember almost nothing. Were you still there?
big_questions.hint: Your body was there, breathing all night. What about your awareness?

story.title: Meenakshi and the Power Cut
story.note: A made-up story. It is true that steady sounds fade from notice, that a change makes us notice again, and that house geckos make clicking calls.
text: Meenakshi lived on the fourth floor of a building in Madurai. She was seven. Her little brother Arjun was five. Their Paati, their grandmother, lived with them.

One evening, Meenakshi was doing her sums at the dining table. Arjun was building a tower of steel tumblers on the floor. The ceiling fan turned above them. Paati was in the kitchen, shelling peas into a bowl.
Then there was a click, and every light went out. The fan slowed down and stopped. "Power cut!" shouted Arjun.
Meenakshi sat very still in the dark. "Paati," she called, "it has gone so quiet. What stopped?"
Paati came in with a torch. "The fan stopped," she said. "And the fridge. The fan was humming all evening."
"But I didn't hear the fan," said Meenakshi. "Not once."
"Your ears heard it," said Paati. "You stopped noticing it. When a sound goes on and on, your mind lets it fade into the background. When it stops, that is a change. So you notice."
Paati sat down on the mat and switched off the torch. "Let's play a noticing game," she said. "Close your eyes. Hold up one finger for every new sound you hear."

At first Meenakshi heard nothing at all. Then a scooter horn beeped down on the road. One finger. A pressure cooker whistled in the flat next door. Two fingers. A crow cawed from the water tank on the roof. Three.
Arjun was still knocking his tumblers together. "Arjun, you are the loudest sound of all," laughed Meenakshi. Arjun stopped.

In the new quiet, Meenakshi heard more. A dog barked far away. Someone's TV was talking very softly. The kitchen tap went drip, drip. Then a small chik-chik-chik came from the wall. "That's the gecko," whispered Paati. Meenakshi had seven fingers up.
"Were all these sounds here before the power cut?" asked Paati.
Meenakshi thought hard. The road had been there all evening. The neighbour cooked every night. The gecko lived behind the calendar. "I think so," she said slowly. "But I was busy with my sums."
"That's it," said Paati. "Your attention was on your sums, so you noticed your sums. Now your attention is on sounds, so you notice sounds."
"Teach me, Akka!" said Arjun. Akka means big sister in Tamil. So Meenakshi taught him. "Shut your eyes. Keep your hands still. Now listen, and hold up a finger for each new sound."
Arjun found the dripping tap and the gecko. Then he found one that Meenakshi had missed: the soft snap of a pea pod in Paati's hands. Meenakshi was surprised. It had been right next to her.
"What does the gecko notice?" asked Arjun.
"The gecko notices her own world," said Paati. "The moths near the window. The warm wall under her feet. She is aware in her own gecko way, and we are aware in ours."
Meenakshi had another question. "Paati, when you hear the cooker whistle, is it the same as when I hear it?"
Paati smiled in the dark. "We both hear it. But I can never get inside your ears to check. All we can do is tell each other what it is like."
Then, with a hum, the lights came back on. The fan began to turn. Meenakshi listened. There it was, the fan's soft whirr, and the fridge buzzing in the kitchen. "I can hear the fan now!" she said.
Ten minutes later, she was back at her sums. When Appa came home, he said, "Is the fan making that noise again?" Meenakshi looked up. She had forgotten all about the fan.
She laughed and took his hand. "Appa, sit down on the mat and close your eyes," she said. "I am going to teach you a game."
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenakshi first thinks the quiet came with the power cut. She finds out that the sounds were there all along, and that her attention decided which ones she noticed. Then she forgets the fan again, which shows how easily we get used to a steady sound.
ask: Why did the flat suddenly seem so quiet in the power cut?
Why did Meenakshi not hear the fan while she did her sums?
Which sound did Arjun find that Meenakshi had missed?
Paati says she can never get inside Meenakshi's ears to check. What does she mean?
What do you think the gecko was noticing?
art: A Madurai flat in the evening: a girl doing sums at a table, a small boy stacking steel tumblers on the floor and a ceiling fan turning.
The same room dark in a power cut, a grandmother holding a torch in the doorway.
A grandmother and two children sitting on a mat in the dark, eyes closed, holding up fingers.
A small gecko on a wall beside a calendar, near a window with moths.
The lights back on, the fan turning, the girl laughing as she pulls her father down onto the mat.

games.title: Noticed It Before? A card game
games.context: This is a card game about things that are often there but rarely noticed. Each card names one. You stop, notice it, and decide which pile it goes on.

printables.title: 12 cards to cut out, with a fact on the back

items.f: The fan's hum
items.b: A steady sound fades from notice after a while. It still reaches your ears.

items.f: Your tongue in your mouth
items.b: Your tongue touches your teeth all day. You notice it only when you think about it.

items.f: The smell of your home
items.b: You stop smelling your own home. Visitors notice its smell at once.

items.f: Your breathing
items.b: Breathing goes on by itself. You can notice it, and slow it down, when you choose.

items.f: Your heartbeat
items.b: Most of the time you hardly feel your heartbeat. Put a hand on your chest after running, and you will.

items.f: Your nose
items.b: Your nose is in front of your eyes all day. Close one eye and look for it.

items.f: Your feet on the floor
items.b: Your feet press on the floor all the time you stand. You notice when you pay attention.

items.f: Blinking
items.b: You blink many times a minute. Each blink makes the world dark for a moment, and you hardly notice.

items.f: Sounds from the road
items.b: A city flat is full of road sounds. You stop noticing them until something changes, such as a horn or a siren.

items.f: Your food being digested
items.b: Your stomach works on your food for hours. You almost never notice it happening.

items.f: Your hair growing
items.b: Your hair grows a little every day. Nobody notices it growing, only that it has grown.

items.f: The light in the room
items.b: You notice the light when it changes: a power cut, a cloud, or someone switching on a lamp.

rules: Make three piles on the floor: 'I was noticing it', 'I notice it now' and 'Hard to notice, even now'.
Mix the cards and put them face down.
Take turns. Pick a card, read the front out loud, and stop for five seconds to notice it.
Put the card on a pile and say why.
Turn the card over and read the fact on the back.
Other players may say if they would choose a different pile, and why. Both answers can be right.
When all the cards are played, count each pile.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and make three paper labels for the piles.
flow.say: Some things are always there, but we hardly notice them. Let's find out which.
flow.kid: Make three piles: 'I was noticing it', 'I notice it now' and 'Hard to notice, even now'.

flow.do: Play, taking turns. Ask for a reason each time.
flow.say: Stop and notice it. Which pile? Why?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Stop and notice it. Which pile? Why?

good: I notice my tongue now, but I wasn't before.
I can't notice my food being digested, even now.

flow.do: Count each pile together.
flow.say: Which pile is biggest? What does that tell us about noticing?
flow.kid: Count each pile. Which is biggest?

ask.q: What does the biggest pile tell us?
good: Lots of things are there that we don't notice.
We notice things when we pay attention.

check.q: You hardly feel your heartbeat, but after running you do. What changed?
options: Your heart only began beating then
Your heart beats harder and faster, so you notice it
check.why: Your heart was beating all along. After running it beats harder and faster. This change catches your attention.

setup.art: Twelve small cards face down on a mat, and three paper labels: 'I was noticing it', 'I notice it now', 'Hard to notice, even now'.
setup.caption: 1. Make three piles and mix the cards.

setup.art: A girl holding a card that says 'Your nose', with one eye closed, looking at her own nose.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card, stop and notice, then choose a pile.

games.title: Awake, Dream, Deep Sleep: a moving game
games.context: This is a moving game. A caller reads a card about a moment in the day or night. Players act out awake, dreaming or deep sleep.

printables.title: 12 caller cards, with the answer on the back

items.f: Amma calls you for breakfast, and you answer.
items.b: Awake. You notice the world around you and answer it.

items.f: You fly over the Howrah Bridge on a giant kite.
items.b: Dream. Your sleeping mind made this world.

items.f: The night passes, and in the morning it feels as if no time went by.
items.b: Deep sleep. You were aware of very little, and remember almost nothing.

items.f: Your teacher turns into a peacock, and you are not surprised.
items.b: Dream. In dreams, strange things often feel normal.

items.f: You count the whistles of the pressure cooker.
items.b: Awake. Your attention is on the cooker.

items.f: You are lying still, breathing slowly, and a soft sound does not wake you.
items.b: Deep sleep. Quiet sounds do not reach your notice.

items.f: You talk to a fish in a Kerala backwater, and the fish talks back.
items.b: Dream. Your mind is making the fish and their voice.

items.f: You taste lemon juice and make a face.
items.b: Awake. You are aware of the sour.

items.f: You run and run but your legs move slowly, as if in thick payasam.
items.b: Dream. Many people have this kind of dream.

items.f: Someone gently tucks a blanket over you, and in the morning you do not know it happened.
items.b: Deep sleep. When you are deeply asleep, very little reaches your notice, even a touch.

items.f: You notice the gecko on the wall and watch her catch a moth.
items.b: Awake. You are noticing another noticer.

items.f: You wake up and say, 'That felt so real!'
items.b: Awake, just after a dream. Dreams usually feel real while we are in them.

rules: Choose a caller. Everyone else stands in a space with room to move.
Awake: walk around and look about. Dream: float your arms slowly like you are flying. Deep sleep: lie down very still.
The caller reads a card out loud.
Players act out awake, dream or deep sleep.
The caller turns the card and reads the answer.

flow.do: Show the three moves.
flow.say: Awake, walk and look about. Dream, float your arms. Deep sleep, lie still as a log.
flow.kid: Awake: walk. Dream: float. Deep sleep: lie still.

flow.do: Play through the cards. After each, read the back.
flow.say: Listen to the card. Awake, dream or deep sleep? Move!
flow.kid: Listen. Awake, dream or deep sleep? Move!

ask.q: How did you know it was a dream?
good: People can't fly on kites.
Strange things felt normal.

flow.do: Finish with everyone lying still.
flow.say: Now everyone lies still, like deep sleep. What are you aware of right now?
flow.kid: Lie still. What are you aware of now?

check.q: In which state do you remember almost nothing afterwards?
check.why: In deep sleep you are aware of very little. In the morning it can feel as if no time passed.

setup.art: Three small pictures: a child walking and looking about, a child floating arms like wings, and a child lying still on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Learn the three moves.

setup.art: A girl reading a card out loud while the other players float their arms.
setup.caption: 2. The caller reads. Everyone moves.

experiments.title: Busy or Still: do you notice more sounds when you pay attention?
experiments.context: In this experiment you count how many sounds you notice in two minutes while racing to sort beans, and in two minutes while sitting still and listening. You do it in two rooms.
experiments.question: Do you notice more sounds when you sit still and listen than when you are busy with a job?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will you notice more sounds while you are busy, while you sit still, or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: In each room, use the same two minutes and the same rule: tell all the sounds you noticed straight after, and count each sound once. The sound of the beans themselves does not count. Only one thing changes: a busy job or sitting still and listening. In the still round, keep your eyes on the bowl of beans, as you did in the busy round. Do the second room in the other order, so going second is not what makes the difference.

materials.item: a small bowl with about 20 rajma beans and 20 chana mixed together (any two kinds of dal, beans or seeds that look different will do)
a phone or clock to time two minutes
paper and a pencil for the results table

schedule.what: Guess, then do a busy round and a still round in one room, and the same in a second room in the other order. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table with the number of sounds for each round. Circle the bigger number in each room.

setup.art: A bowl of mixed red rajma and pale chana on a mat, with two small steel katoris beside it and a phone showing a 2-minute timer.
setup.caption: 1. Mix the beans. Set a timer for two minutes.

setup.art: A girl bent over the bowl, quickly sorting rajma into one katori and chana into the other, with a fan above her.
setup.caption: 2. Busy round: sort the beans as fast as you can.

setup.art: The same girl sitting still on the mat with her hands in her lap, looking at the bowl of beans.
setup.caption: 3. Still round: sit still, look at the bowl and listen.

setup.art: A mother writing two numbers in a table on paper while the girl counts on her fingers.
setup.caption: 4. Straight after each round, tell every sound you noticed.

flow.do: Ask the question. Wait for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the paper.
flow.say: We are going to count sounds. Will you notice more sounds while you are busy, or while you sit still? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess: will you notice more sounds while you are busy, or while you sit still? Why?

good: Still, because I can listen properly.
The same, because the sounds are the same.
Busy, because I will be moving and alert.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine if it has a reason. Do not say what usually happens.

flow.do: 1. Mix the rajma and chana in the bowl. 2. Put the two katoris beside it. 3. Draw the results table with two rooms.
flow.say: In the busy round, you sort rajma into one katori and chana into the other, as fast as you can. In the still round, you only listen.
flow.kid: In the busy round, sort the rajma into one katori and the chana into the other, as fast as you can.

ask.q: What must stay the same in every round?
good: Two minutes each time.
The same room for both rounds.
Tell all the sounds straight after.

flow.do: Room 1, busy round. 1. Start the timer. 2. The child sorts beans for two minutes. 3. Stop. 4. The child tells every sound they noticed. Write the number.
flow.say: Ready? Sort as fast as you can. Keep your eyes on the beans. Stop! Now tell me every sound you noticed.
flow.kid: Sort the beans fast for two minutes. Then tell every sound you heard.
flow.parent: Do not hint at any sound. Count each sound once, even if it came many times. Your own voice saying start and stop does not count, and neither does the sound of the beans.

flow.do: Room 1, still round. 1. Pour the beans back into the bowl and stir them. 2. Start the timer. 3. The child sits still for two minutes, looking at the bowl and listening. 4. The child tells every sound. Write the number.
flow.say: Now sit still. Keep your eyes on the bowl and just listen. Stop! Tell me every sound you noticed.
flow.kid: Sit still. Look at the bowl. Listen for two minutes. Then tell every sound.

flow.do: Room 2, the other order. 1. Move to a second room, for example the kitchen or a bedroom. 2. Do the still round first. 3. Then stir the beans and do the busy round. 4. Write both numbers.
flow.say: This time we do the still round first, then the busy round. Why do you think we swap the order?
flow.kid: New room. Still round first. Then the busy round.

ask.q: Why do we swap the order?
good: In case going second helps you.
So it is fair for both kinds of round.

flow.parent: If the flat is very quiet, switch on the fan in both rounds of a room, or open a window. Sounds in a city flat are usually the fan, the fridge, traffic, horns, birds, neighbours, a lift and the water motor.

flow.do: Look at the table together. In each room, circle the bigger number.
flow.say: Look at your table. In which round did you notice more sounds? Was it the same in both rooms? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Look at your numbers. Which round was bigger? Was your guess right?

good: I noticed 2 sounds busy and 8 sounds still.
Still was bigger in both rooms.

flow.parent: Most children notice two or three times as many sounds when still. If busy came out the same or bigger, ask why. Perhaps they listened while sorting. That is a real finding too. Only after the child has said what they saw, read the card on attention.

flow.do: Ask about one steady sound, such as the fan or fridge, that was on in both rounds.
flow.say: Was the fan running in the busy round too? Did you notice it then? So did the room change, or did something in you change?
flow.kid: Was the fan on in the busy round too? Did you notice it?

good: Where I put my attention.
I was listening in the still round.

flow.think: The sounds were the same in both rounds. What was different?

experiments.title: Same Lemon, Different Sour: does everyone feel the same sour?
experiments.context: In this experiment everyone at home tastes three drops of the same lemon juice. Each person shows with their fingers how sour it felt, without looking at anyone else.
experiments.question: If everyone tastes the same lemon juice, will everyone show the same amount of sour?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will everyone hold up the same number of fingers, or different numbers? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use one lemon, three drops on a clean spoon for each person, and the same finger scale from 1 for a little sour to 5 for very sour. Everyone shuts their eyes and shows fingers at the same moment, so nobody copies anyone.
results_table: One word for how it felt

materials.item: a clean steel spoon for each person
a glass of water for each person, to rinse the mouth afterwards
paper and a pencil for the results table

schedule.what: Guess, then everyone tastes three drops and shows sour fingers with eyes shut. Write the numbers and words. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then circle anyone whose number was different from yours.

setup.art: Half a lemon being squeezed over a steel spoon, three drops falling.
setup.caption: 1. Put three drops of lemon juice on each spoon.

setup.art: Three family members sitting in a row with eyes shut, each holding up a different number of fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Taste, shut your eyes, and show 1 to 5 fingers on 'three'.

setup.art: A girl writing numbers and words in a table: 2 sharp, 4 sour, 5 ouch.
setup.caption: 3. Write everyone's fingers and one word each.

flow.do: Ask the question. Wait for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Everyone will taste the same lemon. Will everyone show the same number of sour fingers? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Everyone tastes the same lemon. Will everyone show the same number of fingers? Why?

good: The same, because it is the same lemon.
Different, because some people like sour things.
Different, because people are different.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine if it has a reason. Ask everyone at home who is willing to taste. Skip anyone who has a mouth ulcer or does not want to.

flow.do: 1. Show the finger scale: 1 finger is a little sour, 5 fingers is very sour. 2. Squeeze three drops onto each spoon.
flow.say: One finger means a little sour. Five fingers means very, very sour. Three drops each, on your own spoon.
flow.kid: One finger is a little sour. Five is very sour.

flow.do: 1. Everyone tastes their drops. 2. Everyone shuts their eyes. 3. Count to three. 4. Everyone shows fingers. 5. Write each number down. Then everyone sips water.
flow.say: Taste it. Now shut your eyes. One, two, three: show your fingers! Keep them up while I write.
flow.kid: Taste it. Shut your eyes. On three, show your fingers.
flow.parent: Eyes shut stops people copying each other. Write the numbers before anyone opens their eyes.

flow.do: Each person says one word for how the sour felt. Write it next to their number.
flow.say: Say one word for how it felt. Sharp? Tingly? Ouch? Nice?
flow.kid: Say one word for how it felt.

flow.do: Look at the table together.
flow.say: Did everyone show the same number? If two of us both showed four, did we feel the same sour? How could we check?
flow.kid: Did everyone show the same? Can you check someone else's sour?

ask.q: Can we know if two fours feel the same?
good: No, I can only feel my own sour.
We can only tell each other in words and fingers.

flow.parent: Numbers usually differ a little. If everyone showed the same, the question still stands: is your four the same as mine? There is no way to check from the outside. That is the point of the test. Only after the child has said what they think, read the card on what it is like to be you.
flow.think: Your sour is yours. How do other people find out about it?

activities.title: The Sound That Went Away
activities.context: In this activity a soft, steady sound plays while you draw. Then it stops. You find out whether you notice the stop, and whether you were noticing the sound before.

materials.item: a phone that can play a soft, steady sound, such as rain or a tanpura drone, on low volume (a ticking clock also works)

schedule.what: Draw for five minutes with a soft sound playing. A grown-up stops it quietly. Talk about what you noticed.

activities.record: Write yes or no: I noticed when the sound stopped. Write yes or no: I was hearing it just before it stopped.

setup.art: A phone on a shelf playing soft rain sounds, with small sound marks, and a girl drawing at a table.
setup.caption: 1. Play a soft, steady sound. Start drawing.

setup.art: A mother quietly pressing stop on the phone while the girl looks up from her drawing.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up stops the sound without saying anything.

flow.do: Start a soft, steady sound on the phone. Do not say anything about it.
flow.say: Here is some paper. Draw your favourite place for five minutes.
flow.kid: Draw your favourite place.

flow.do: Let the child draw. After about four minutes, quietly stop the sound.
flow.say: Keep drawing.
flow.kid: Keep drawing.
flow.parent: Do not look at the phone when you stop it. Watch the child's face.

flow.do: Ask the two questions.
flow.say: Did anything change just now? Before it stopped, were you hearing the sound?
flow.kid: Did something change? Were you hearing it before?

ask.q: Were you hearing the sound before it stopped?
good: I forgot about it, but I noticed when it stopped.
No, but the quiet felt different.

flow.parent: Most children notice the stop, yet say they had stopped hearing the sound. This is getting used to it, or habituation. The sound kept reaching their ears all along. That is how they could notice it stop. If your child did not notice the stop, that is a real finding too: they were fully busy with the drawing.

activities.title: Watch a Noticer: what does another being notice?
activities.context: In this activity you quietly watch an ant, a crow, a pigeon, a gecko or a fly for five minutes, and draw what they seem to notice.

materials.item: a being to watch: ants on the kitchen floor, a crow or pigeon at the window, or a gecko on the wall

schedule.what: Watch one being for five minutes from a little way off. Draw them, and draw what they turned towards or moved away from.

activities.record: A drawing of the being, with arrows to what they noticed.

setup.art: A girl sitting still a little way from a line of ants on a kitchen floor, watching.
setup.caption: 1. Find a being and sit still, a little way off.

setup.art: A drawing of a crow on a ledge with arrows to a crumb and to a child at the window.
setup.caption: 2. Draw them, with arrows to what they noticed.

flow.do: Help the child find a being to watch. Ants, crows, pigeons and geckos are found in most city flats.
flow.say: Let's find someone to watch. An ant, a crow or a gecko. We watch quietly, so we don't disturb them.
flow.kid: Find an ant, a crow or a gecko. Sit still.

flow.do: Watch together for five minutes. Talk in whispers.
flow.say: What do they turn towards? What do they move away from? What makes them stop?
flow.kid: Watch. What do they turn to? What do they run from?

good: The crow turned her head when I moved.
The ants went round a drop of water.

flow.parent: If no animal turns up, watch a potted plant instead and talk about how plants notice light over days.

flow.do: The child draws the being, with arrows to what they noticed.
flow.say: Draw them. Draw an arrow to each thing they noticed.
flow.kid: Draw them. Add arrows to what they noticed.
flow.think: Was the ant noticing you, the way you were noticing the ant?

activities.title: Five Things Right Now: a counting-down noticing game
activities.context: In this activity you notice 5 things you see, 4 you hear, 3 you feel touching you, 2 you smell and 1 you taste, wherever you are.

materials.item: nothing but you, in any room

schedule.what: Count down from 5 to 1 with your senses, then count how many things you noticed in all.

activities.record: Write how many things you noticed in all.

setup.art: A hand showing five fingers, then four, then three, then two, then one, each with a small picture of an eye, ear, hand, nose and tongue.
setup.caption: 1. Five you see, four you hear, three you feel.

setup.art: A boy sitting on a balcony sniffing the air, with a tulsi plant beside him.
setup.caption: 2. Two you smell, one you taste.

flow.do: Lead the child through the five steps, one at a time.
flow.say: Tell me five things you can see. Now four things you can hear. Three things you can feel touching you. Two things you can smell. One thing you can taste.
flow.kid: Name five things you see, four you hear, three you feel touching you, two you smell and one you taste.

flow.do: Add up the things together.
flow.say: How many things did you notice in all? Were you noticing them before we started?
flow.kid: Add them up. Were you noticing them before?

good: 15, because 5 and 4 and 3 and 2 and 1 make 15.

activities.title: Draw Last Night's Dream
activities.context: In this activity, first thing in the morning, you draw a dream you remember and talk about who was noticing it.

materials.item: paper and crayons, kept beside the bed

schedule.what: In the morning, before getting up, draw a dream you remember. If you remember none, draw the dream you would like.

activities.record: The dream drawing, with one sentence about it.

setup.art: A girl sitting up in bed in the morning drawing on a paper on her knees.
setup.caption: 1. In the morning, draw your dream.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a girl riding a flying elephant over a city.
setup.caption: 2. Tell someone what happened in it.

flow.do: Give the child paper and crayons as soon as they wake.
flow.say: Did you have a dream? Draw it before it goes. If no dream comes back, draw a dream you would like.
flow.kid: Draw your dream. If you forgot, draw one you would like.
flow.parent: Dreams fade quickly after waking, so do this before breakfast. Many children remember no dream. That is normal. Almost everyone dreams every night.

flow.do: Talk about the drawing.
flow.say: In your dream, did it feel real? Your body was lying in bed. So who was noticing the dream?
flow.kid: Did it feel real? Who was noticing the dream?

good: I was.
My mind, while my body slept.

projects.title: My Noticing Diary: five days, five senses
projects.context: In this project you spend ten minutes a day noticing with one sense, and draw one thing at home you had never noticed before.

materials.item: five sheets of paper folded and tied with thread into a small book

schedule.what: Seeing: find one thing in your home you have never noticed before, and draw it.
Hearing: sit still at a window for two minutes, then draw the sound you had never noticed before.
Touch: feel five surfaces with your eyes shut, and draw the one that surprised you.
Smell: smell five things in the kitchen with your eyes shut, such as jeera, coffee, coconut, a lemon and soap. Draw your favourite.
Taste: eat one small piece of fruit very slowly, and draw how the taste changed.

projects.record: The five-page diary, with one drawing and one sentence a day. The child says the sentence and a grown-up can write it.

setup.art: Five sheets of paper folded and tied with a thread into a little book with 'My Noticing Diary' on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Make a five-page diary.

setup.art: An open page with a drawing of a crack in a wall shaped like a river, and one sentence under it.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, draw one new thing you noticed.

flow.do: Day 1. Make the five-page diary. Then do the seeing page.
flow.say: Today you are a noticing detective. Find one thing in our home that you have never noticed before.
flow.kid: Find one thing at home you never noticed. Draw it.

flow.do: Days 2 and 3. Do the hearing page and the touch page.
flow.say: Sit at the window and listen. Which sound is new to you? Now feel things with your eyes shut.
flow.kid: Listen at the window. Then feel things with eyes shut. Draw one each day.

flow.do: Day 4. Do the smell page. Hold each jar or spice near the child's nose, eyes shut.
flow.say: Smell this with your eyes shut. What is it? Which smell do you like best?
flow.kid: Smell with your eyes shut. Guess each one.

flow.do: Day 5. Do the taste page, then look back at the whole book.
flow.say: Eat this piece very slowly. Does the taste change? Which day did you notice the most?
flow.kid: Eat it slowly. Does the taste change? Look at your book.

ask.q: Why did you find new things in a home you know so well?
good: Because I was paying attention.
I had got used to them, so I stopped noticing.

challenges.title: A Sign Nobody Can Miss
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. People stop noticing anything that never changes. So a reminder sign stuck on a wall soon stops working.
challenges.problem: Your family keeps forgetting to switch off the bathroom light. Make a reminder that they will still notice on the third day.
constraints: Use only things from home, such as paper, crayons, string and tape.
It must still work on the third day, not only the first.
materials: a paper strip or a ribbon
general: A big, bright sign at eye level next to the switch.
A sign with a picture of a light bulb and the word OFF.
creative: Change the sign's colour or picture every day, so nobody gets used to it.
Hang a paper strip from the door frame that brushes your head as you walk out, so you feel the reminder.
challenges.your_turn: Make your own reminder. First, count how many times the light is left on in one evening with no sign. Then put your reminder up, and each evening for three days count again. Did your reminder still work on day 3?

flow.do: Read the challenge together.
flow.say: Why do people stop noticing a sign after a few days?
flow.kid: Why do people stop noticing a sign?

good: They get used to it.
It never changes, so it fades into the background.

flow.do: The child designs and makes a reminder.
flow.say: How can you make a sign that keeps being noticed, even on day three?
flow.kid: Make a reminder people will still notice on day three.

flow.do: Put it up. Agree how you will count for three days.
flow.say: Each evening, we check the light. Will your reminder still work on day three?
flow.kid: Put it up. Check the light each evening for three days.
flow.think: What makes something hard to get used to?

setup.art: A bathroom door with a bright paper sign of a light bulb and the word OFF next to the switch.
setup.caption: 1. Make a sign or reminder.

setup.art: A paper ribbon hanging from a door frame, brushing the head of a girl walking out.
setup.caption: 2. Or make a reminder that you feel as you walk past.

videos.title: The selective attention test (the gorilla film)
videos.why: Watch this after the sound test. Your child counts ball passes and may miss something surprising.
videos.check: Found by search: "selective attention test" by Daniel Simons, 1 minute 22 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Why do we stop noticing smells after a while?
videos.why: Watch this after the Sound That Went Away activity. It explains how we get used to a steady smell, which happens in the same way as with a steady sound.
videos.check: Found by search: "Why Do You Stop Noticing Smells After A While?" by BrainStuff - HowStuffWorks, 3 minutes 35 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Why do we dream?
videos.why: Watch this after the Awake, Dream, Deep Sleep game. It explains why we dream during sleep.
videos.check: Found by search: "Why Do We Dream?" by SciShow Kids, 4 minutes 40 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: What does it mean to be aware of something?
opts: You know or feel that it is there
quiz.why: Being aware means knowing or feeling that something is there. Being aware of anything at all is called consciousness.

quiz.p: In the sound test, when do most children notice more sounds?
quiz.why: When you sit still and listen, your attention is on sounds, so you notice many more.

quiz.p: Why did we do the sound test in two rooms, in a different order each time?
opts: So that going second is not what made the difference
Because the first room was too noisy
quiz.why: If the still round wins in both rooms, whichever round came first, then going second was not the reason.

quiz.p: You are reading a story and do not hear your name called. Why?
opts: Your attention is on the story
quiz.why: Attention picks what you notice. Your ears heard the call, but your attention was on the story.

quiz.p: The fan hums all evening. Why do you stop noticing it?
opts: Your mind lets a steady sound fade from notice
quiz.why: This is getting used to it, or habituation. The sound still reaches your ears.

quiz.p: In a power cut the fan suddenly stops. What usually happens?
opts: You notice the quiet at once
quiz.why: A change catches your attention. The stop is a change, so you notice it.

quiz.p: True or false: two people tasting the same lemon always feel exactly the same sour.
quiz.why: False. In the lemon test people often show different numbers. Even with the same number, nobody can check that their sours feel alike.

quiz.p: In the lemon test, you show 4 fingers for the sour. How can someone else learn what your sour was like?
opts: From what you tell and show them
quiz.why: Only you have your experience. Others learn about it from your words, face and fingers.

quiz.p: You walk up the wall and across the ceiling, and it does not seem strange at all. Which state are you in?
quiz.why: In dreams, strange things often feel normal. Your sleeping mind is making this world.

quiz.p: In which state are you aware of very little, and remember almost nothing later?
quiz.why: In deep sleep you are aware of very little. In the morning it can feel as if no time went by.

quiz.p: Which of these notice their world?
opts: An ant, a crow, a tulsi plant and you
quiz.why: Every being notices their world in their own way. Some scientists say only beings with brains are aware, and this is still argued about.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not know?
opts: How and why being aware happens at all
Whether steady sounds fade from notice
quiz.why: Nobody knows how or why awareness happens. The other two have been tested many times.

items.p: Draw yourself in the still round of the sound test. Draw three sounds you noticed around you.
items.a: A child sitting still and looking at the bowl of beans, and three sound makers such as a fan, a crow and a car.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the child still, and real sounds from their own test.

items.p: Choosing what to notice is called your ___.
items.why: Attention picks out a small part of everything your senses take in.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: knowing or feeling that something is there
what something is like for you
items.why: These three words are the heart of this unit.

items.p: Sort these sounds into steady sounds we stop noticing, and sudden sounds we notice at once.
items.why: We get used to sounds that go on without changing. A sudden sound is a change, so we notice it.

items.p: In the sound test, why did you notice more sounds when you sat still? Say it out loud and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: Because my attention was on the sounds, not on the beans.
items.why: A strong answer says the sounds were the same, and only where the attention went changed.

items.p: This picture shows Meenakshi from the story Meenakshi and the Power Cut. Draw an arrow to what she is noticing, and one to a sound she is not noticing.
labels: a sound she is not noticing
items.why: Her attention is on her sums. The fan's sound reaches her, but she has got used to it.
items.art: A girl bent over sums in a notebook at a table, with a ceiling fan turning above her.

items.p: Name one sound at home that you hardly ever notice. How could you make yourself notice it? Say it out loud and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: For example: the fridge hum. I could sit still, shut my eyes and listen for it.
items.why: A strong answer names a real steady sound and says that paying attention, or a change, makes us notice it.

items.p: In the lemon test, people showed different numbers of fingers for the same lemon. What does this tell us?
opts: Some of them tasted it wrongly
Each person has their own experience, and we learn about it by being told
The lemon changed for each person
items.why: Only you have your own sour. Other people learn about it from your words, your face and your fingers.

items.p: In a dream, you fly like a bird. Where is your body?
items.why: In a dream you are aware of a world your sleeping mind makes. Your body stays in bed.

items.p: True or false: almost everyone dreams every night, even people who forget their dreams.
items.why: True. People woken during dreaming sleep in sleep laboratories usually say they were dreaming, even if they forget their dreams at home.

items.p: Nandini, aged 7, and her Thatha tasted the same lemon juice in the lemon test.

views.says: We tasted the same lemon, so we felt the same sour. You just show your fingers differently.
I showed 5 fingers and you showed 2. So we felt different sours.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other person has right. Say it out loud and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. Nandini has evidence: the numbers were different. Thatha has a point too: one person's 5 may not mean the same as another person's 5. Nobody can check from the outside.
items.why: Both views are real. This is why scientists find experience so hard to study.

items.p: Suppose you do the sound test in one room only, with the busy round first and the still round second. The still round wins. What else could explain it?
opts: In the second round you already knew to listen for sounds
items.why: Going second may have helped. That is why the test is done again in a second room, in the other order.

items.p: Someone says, 'I didn't hear the fan, so the fan made no sound.' What would you tell them? Say it out loud and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: The fan was making a sound, but they had got used to it. If it stopped, they would notice.
items.why: A strong answer says that not noticing a sound is different from no sound, and gives a way to show it, such as switching the fan off.

items.p: True or false: you can feel exactly what your friend feels when she tastes a lemon.
items.why: False. Only she has her experience. You learn about it from her words, her face and her fingers.

items.p: Draw an ant on the kitchen floor. Draw arrows to three things you think the ant notices.
items.a: An ant with arrows to things such as a crumb, a drop of water and another ant.
items.why: A strong drawing shows things an ant could really sense nearby, such as food smells and other ants.

items.p: Put the steps of the lemon test in order.
items: shut your eyes and show fingers on three
put three drops on a spoon
say one word for how it felt
a: put three drops on a spoon
shut your eyes and show fingers on three
say one word for how it felt
items.why: First guess, then taste, then show the score without copying, then describe it.

items.p: Sort these into Awake, Dreaming and Deep sleep.
items: a night that seems to pass in no time
talking to a fish who answers
items.why: Awake, you notice the world. Dreaming, you notice a world your mind makes. In deep sleep you are aware of very little.

items.p: Draw a line from each being to something they notice.
items.why: Every being notices their world in their own way.

items.p: When a sound goes on and on without changing, you get ___ to it and stop noticing it.
items.why: Getting used to something is called habituation.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? Seeing, hearing, smelling, deep sleep.
items.why: Seeing, hearing and smelling are ways of noticing the world. In deep sleep you are aware of very little.

items.p: Many people think we notice everything in front of us. Plan a test at home to check. What would you do? Say it out loud and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: For example: ask a grown-up to count how many times a ball is passed, while someone walks past with a pillow on their head. Then ask if they saw anything odd.
items.why: A strong plan gives the watcher a busy job, adds something unusual, and asks afterwards. That is how Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris did their gorilla test.

items.p: Two scientists are talking about a touch-me-not plant, who folds her leaves when touched.

views.says: The touch-me-not senses a touch and folds. The medicine that makes people unaware for an operation stops her folding too. She is aware in her own way.
Awareness needs a brain. The plant has none. The folding is an automatic response.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say one thing the other scientist has right. Say it out loud and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses evidence: the medicine result, or the fact that brains change awareness in people. Then it says what the other side has right.
items.why: Scientists really do argue about this. Both use real evidence.

items.p: Suppose you do the busy round in a noisy room in the day, and the still round in a quiet room at night. The busy round wins. Can you say that being busy helps you notice sounds?
opts: No, because the room and the time changed too
Yes, because night is always quiet
items.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. Here the noisy room simply had more sounds in it.

items.p: True or false: scientists know exactly how being aware happens.
items.why: False. Nobody knows how or why being aware happens at all. This is one of the biggest open questions in science.

items.p: A child did the still round of the sound test in three rooms. The child noticed 6, 7 and 8 sounds. How many sounds is that in all?
items.why: 6 + 7 + 8 = 21. In the busy rounds the child noticed 2, 3 and 1, which is only 6 in all.

items.p: Label the three pictures: awake, dreaming and deep sleep.
a: the child brushing teeth is awake
the child with a dream cloud is dreaming
the child asleep with no cloud is in deep sleep
items.why: Each picture shows a different way of being aware, or of being aware of very little.
items.art: Three panels: a child brushing teeth at a sink, a child asleep with a dream cloud of a flying kite, and a child asleep under a dark sky with no cloud.

items.p: If you stop noticing the smell of your own home, has the smell gone? How could a visitor help you find out? Say it out loud and a grown-up can write it down.
items.a: No. The smell is still there. A visitor who has not got used to it can tell you what they smell.
items.why: A strong answer says that getting used to a smell is different from the smell going, and uses someone fresh to check.

items.p: Which of these shows that the fan's sound still reaches you when you are not noticing it?
opts: You notice at once when the fan stops
items.why: If the sound was not reaching you, you could not notice the change when it stops.

items.p: Sort these things your body does into 'I usually notice' and 'I usually do not notice'.
items.why: Your body does a great deal without your noticing. Changes, such as a bite or a sneeze, catch your attention.

items.p: In 1960, Anne Treisman, a student at Oxford, played one story into each ear and swapped the stories halfway. Many people followed their story into the wrong ear for a word or two. What did this show?
opts: The ear they ignored was shut out completely
Some meaning from the ignored ear still gets through
People cannot hear with two ears
items.why: If the ignored ear were shut out like a closed door, nobody could follow a story into it. Its sounds are turned down, not shut out.

applications: Traffic lights, ambulance sirens and road signs are made bright, flashing or changing, so drivers notice them.
Doctors called anaesthetists use medicines that make a person unaware during an operation, then let their awareness come back.
Many alarms beep in a changing pattern, because people stop noticing a sound that stays the same.
Teachers clap a rhythm or ring a bell to catch a class's attention.
Some schools teach children to notice their breath for a minute, to help them settle and pay attention.

spotted.text: In a Hyderabad flat, everyone notices the sudden quiet when the fan stops in a power cut.
spotted.art: A family in a dark flat looking up at a ceiling fan that has just stopped.

spotted.text: A flower seller in a busy Chennai market hears her own name through all the noise.
spotted.art: A woman at a flower stall with jasmine strings turning her head as someone calls her name across a crowded market.

spotted.text: A crow on a Kochi balcony turns her head the moment a steel plate clinks.
spotted.art: A crow on a balcony railing turning her head towards a kitchen window.

spotted.text: A tulsi plant on a Pune windowsill leans towards the light.
spotted.art: A tulsi plant in a pot on a windowsill, leaning towards the bright window.

spotted.text: In Guwahati homes, many mothers say they sleep through thunder but wake at their baby's small cry.

open_questions.q: How does being aware happen at all?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can see which parts of the brain are busy when people notice things. Nobody knows how or why that comes with an experience. The philosopher David Chalmers called this the hard problem in 1995.

open_questions.q: Which beings are aware, and what is it like to be them?
open_questions.why_open: We can watch what a bee or a plant does. We cannot step inside their experience. Scientists still argue about how to test this.

open_questions.q: Is your red the same as my red?
open_questions.why_open: We both call a tomato red and agree on which things are red. There is no known way to check whether the colour looks the same inside each of us.
Scientists have many ideas, such as sorting memories or practising for danger. None has been proved.

maths.problem: In the sound test, you noticed 3 sounds in the busy round and 8 sounds in the still round, in the same room. How many more sounds did you notice when still?
maths.explain: 8 take away 3 is 5. You noticed many more sounds when your attention was on sounds.
maths.context: This is about the sound test, where you counted sounds while busy and while still.
maths.why_maths: Taking one number from the other shows how big the difference is, not just which is bigger.

maths.problem: Four friends, Ananya, Bilal, Chitra and Deepa, did the still round of the sound test. They made tally marks for the sounds they noticed: Ananya 7, Bilal 6, Chitra 3, Deepa 9. Who noticed the most sounds? Who noticed the fewest?
maths.answer: Deepa noticed the most, with 9. Chitra noticed the fewest, with 3.
maths.explain: Put them in order: 3, 6, 7, 9. The biggest is 9 and the smallest is 3.
maths.context: This is about the sound test, done by four friends.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks let you count sounds quickly while someone is saying them out loud.

maths.problem: The sound test was done in four rooms. Busy rounds: 2, 3, 1, 2 sounds. Still rounds: 7, 6, 8, 5 sounds. In how many rooms did the still round win? What does that tell you that one room alone could not?
maths.answer: The still round won in all 4 rooms. So it was not a fluke of one room.
maths.explain: Compare each pair: 7 is more than 2, 6 is more than 3, 8 is more than 1, 5 is more than 2. The same pattern four times makes it much more likely to be real.
maths.context: This is about the sound test, done in four rooms.
maths.why_maths: Comparing pairs of numbers shows whether a pattern holds every time.

maths.problem: In the lemon test, five people showed 3, 4, 4, 2 and 5 fingers. How many people showed more than 3? Does that mean the lemon tasted more sour to them?
maths.answer: 3 people showed more than 3. We can't be sure the lemon tasted more sour to them, because one person's 4 may not feel the same as another's 4.
maths.explain: 4, 4 and 5 are more than 3. That is 3 people. But each number only stands for how the sour felt to one person, and nobody else can feel that person's sour.
maths.context: This is about the lemon test, where everyone showed sour fingers from 1 to 5.
maths.why_maths: Counting helps us see the pattern, and thinking about what the numbers mean stops us reading too much into them.

maths.problem: In Five Things Right Now, you notice 5 things you see, 4 you hear, 3 you feel, 2 you smell and 1 you taste. How many things is that in all?
maths.context: This is about the Five Things Right Now game, where you count down with your senses.
maths.why_maths: Adding the counts shows how many things were there to notice in one ordinary moment.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1953, Colin Cherry, a British scientist, played two different spoken messages to people at once, one in each ear. He asked them to repeat one message aloud. Afterwards they could say almost nothing about the other message. In 1958, Donald Broadbent explained this with an idea: the mind shuts out the ear you are not listening to, like closing a door. Then new tests showed that the door idea was not quite right. In 1959, Neville Moray found that some people heard their own name in the shut-out ear. In 1960, a young student at Oxford, Anne Treisman, tried a clever test. She played a story into one ear and a different story into the other. Halfway through, she swapped the stories over. Many people followed their story into the wrong ear for a word or two, without meaning to. So the ignored ear had not been shut out. Its sounds were turned down, and some of their meaning still got through. Treisman went on to become one of the best-known scientists of attention in the world.
how_we_found_out.who: Colin Cherry, Donald Broadbent and Neville Moray in England, and Anne Treisman at the University of Oxford
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the mind shuts out everything you are not paying attention to, like a closed door. Moray's own-name finding and Treisman's swapped-story test showed that ignored sounds are turned down, not shut out.
how_we_found_out.art: A young woman scientist in the 1960s with big headphones on a table, a reel-to-reel tape recorder, and two speech bubbles crossing from one ear to the other.

roots.context: In the sound test, we counted the sounds we noticed when busy and when sitting still. In the lemon test, we found out what the same lemon is like for each of us. Now we ask what these two tests tell us about being aware.

deep_truth.truth: In the sound test, while you were busy sorting beans, you noticed only a few sounds. Sitting still in the same room, you noticed many more. The sounds were the same, and only your attention changed. So what you are aware of depends on where you put your attention.
deep_truth.habit: We think we are aware of everything around us, as if our ears and eyes were open windows. The sound test shows that attention picks out only some of it.
deep_truth.evidence: In the sound test, you noticed far more sounds in the still round than in the busy round, in both rooms and in either order.

three.who_am_i: You are the one who notices. Right now you can choose to notice your breath, a sound or your feet.
three.what_is_life: Being alive means noticing your world and answering it: an ant notices a crumb, a plant notices the light, you notice a horn.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of sounds, smells and sights at every moment. Each being notices a different part of it.

roots.thread: At any moment there is one world of sound in your flat. You, a grown-up at home, a crow on the ledge and an ant on the floor each notice a different part of it. Each of them is aware in their own way. Some thinkers say awareness runs through all of them, and through everything, down to the smallest particle. So one world is being noticed in countless ways at once.

teachings.teaching: This Upanishad describes three states: waking, when we are aware of the world outside; dreaming, when we are aware of a world inside; and deep sleep, when we are aware of almost nothing. It names a fourth state, turiya: the awareness that is there through all three.
teachings.link: In this unit you sorted moments into awake, dreaming and deep sleep. Sleep scientists also find that awareness changes through a night.

teachings.source: Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha's teaching on mindfulness (Majjhima Nikaya 10)
teachings.teaching: The Buddha taught: when walking, know that you are walking. When breathing in, know that you are breathing in.
teachings.link: This is attention on purpose. It is what you did in the still round of the sound test, when you noticed sounds you had been missing.

teachings.teaching: The Chinese thinker Zhuangzi dreamt he was a butterfly, happily flying about. When he woke, he wondered: was he Zhuangzi who had dreamt of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming of being Zhuangzi?
teachings.link: A dream feels real while you are in it. Only you have your experience, so it is hard for anyone else to check what it was like.

science.text: Attention picks out a small part of everything your senses take in. Many experiments since the 1950s show this.
Nobody knows how or why being aware happens at all. The philosopher David Chalmers called this the hard problem in 1995.

other_view.who: Most brain scientists today, and the Charvaka thinkers of ancient India
other_view.view: Most brain scientists think awareness is something brains do, so beings without brains are not aware. The Charvaka thinkers taught long ago that awareness comes from the body and ends with it.

practice.title: The Last of the Sound
practice.say: Sit comfortably and close your eyes. I will tap this steel tumbler once with a spoon. Listen as the sound gets softer and softer. Raise your hand when it is gone. Keep your eyes closed. What is the next sound you notice? And the next?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Someone taps a steel tumbler. Listen to the sound fade. Raise your hand when it is gone. What do you notice next?

founder: ideas/by_topic/what-is-real.md was read. The Grade 1 and Grade 2 consciousness grid (being awake and noticing; attention, memory, sensation; dreams feel real though the body sleeps; do animals think like us; awareness connects the world inside and outside) shaped the sound test, the dream game and the noticing activities.
The founder's Week 5.0 journey 'All perception is subjective' shaped the lemon test, which asks whether two people's experience of the same thing can be compared.
Obaid Siddiqi's SCI card (how flies sense taste and smell) and the J.C. Bose journal pages are kept for Level 4, which goes deeper into other minds.

No board chapter is listed for this subtopic. It leads on to sci.what-is-real.consciousness.L4 (subjective experience and what makes you you) and sits beside sci.mind.sense-of-self.L2 and sci.health.sleep.L2 without repeating their tests (the tickle test, the glove hand, the voice recording, sleeping on picture pairs).
